s10.title: Behind the Bumpers | 5727 Omegabytes | Charged Up Robot Overview

bet.text: Design for repairability, and keep the center of gravity low while the arm reaches far enough to place on the high node.

demand.text: At kickoff the team noted that up to seven pieces could be placed in auto and that about two thirds of the mid and high nodes take cones, and talked about earning ranking points alone. At Mecklenburg its goal for each match was four ranking points.

auto.text: Autos combine about 15 base paths with dashboard choices of what to pick up and where to place it, to fit partners.
At the championship it ran one mid cone, one mid cube and one high cube every match and says it missed once.

cycle.text: The arm goes to set points while the intake stays facing forward; rollers spin opposite ways for cones and cubes, and LEDs show yellow or purple.
All controls are on one controller. At the championship the team reports an average of eleven or more cycles a match and no missed high cone.

endgame.text: A four-ranking-point Mecklenburg practice match showed the team it could do four links and engage at the end; four ranking points became its goal for each match. In the third final there it completed a triple climb.

fallback.text: In the Mecklenburg finals, when the intake stopped the team tried pushing pieces into the low nodes; when the arm would not move it played defense.

changed.text: After Asheville the intake grew from 10 in to 16 in and the upper arm from one tube to two. Gas struts went on the upper arm for the state championship and on the lower arm for the world championship, making the arm faster and smoother. At Asheville a damaged CAN wire in the upper arm took two matches to find, and all eight arm positions were recalibrated.

outcome.text: 40-23-2 in official play; ranked 18 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 70.23, Curie).

solves.text: Reach the high node within the extension rules while keeping the center of gravity low

facts.text: At mid-build, #25 chain on the upper and lower arm and #35 on the lower arm pivot; a chain was added with the second upper-arm tube
Upper arm is two 1 x 2 in tubes, each of length
Two 20 lb gas struts on the upper arm, then two more on the lower arm for the world championship
Moves to set points with profiled PID, with feedforward described at Mecklenburg as coming soon; at Asheville a barely tuned PID controller made it jerky

cost.text: After replacing a CANcoder the team had to recalibrate all eight arm positions

solves.text: Keep the intake facing forward through every arm movement

facts.text: At mid-build it ran on #25 chain; belts were considered to save weight
The chain lines up with the arm's hex shaft, so the intake always faces forward

functions.name: Intake

solves.text: Handle cones and cubes with a wider range of vertical lineup error

functions.type: reversing roller intake for cones and cubes

facts.text: 1/8 in polycarbonate pieces cut on the team's router; seven versions were cut
At mid-build, one NEO 550 drives the middle bar and a twisted sewing machine belt reverses the upper bar
Testing showed one wheel was enough for cubes
Width, up from 10 in at Asheville
Rollers spin in opposite directions for cones and cubes; LEDs show which

cost.text: In testing, a three-wheel version set too close to the ground caught the carpet and skipped

solves.text: Keep the center of gravity extra low

functions.name: Arm motor area

solves.text: Collect the arm's mechanisms at the bottom of the robot

functions.type: arm motors and gearing grouped low on the robot

facts.text: Paired motors share a hex shaft; one pair swings the arm and another moves the second arm
The team says most of what is likely to break is in this one area

functions.name: Swerve base
functions.type: swerve with absolute CANcoders on its own CAN loop

facts.text: Two CAN loops: one for the arm and one, on a CANivore, for the swerve; XT30 connectors
At Asheville one CANcoder wire unplugged; the connectors had no zip ties

cost.text: In a state championship playoff match the swerve loop filled with CAN errors and the swerve did not work; after a roboRIO reboot errors and wrong module angles remained, after a power-off everything worked, and the team did not know the cause
A reply is not certain that the power cycle rather than the roboRIO reboot was the fix

functions.name: Autonomous routines

solves.text: Change the auto to fit an alliance partner

functions.type: odometry path following with dashboard choices

facts.text: About 15 base paths give over 200 usable autos
The build thread counts more than 640 selectable routines and nine run at Mecklenburg
The team says paths land within inches of real measurements

decisions.choice: Arm motors and gearing in one low area
decisions.because: most of what is likely to break is in one place, and the mechanisms are collected at the bottom
it keeps the center of gravity extra low

decisions.choice: Two-joint arm on chains, with weight savings as a top priority
decisions.because: the center of gravity had to be as low as possible
testing found it very consistent and more tolerant of vertical lineup error
decisions.instead_of: a mecanum intake that centers cones, left unbuilt for wheel weight and the lineup accuracy it needed

decisions.because: it was the team's first arm since its 2015 rookie year and there were few open examples
the team could not get a Limelight in time
a second coach with a tablet tracks links and calls who places what where
